Hormuz: Iran says three tankers hit its mines on Saturday, Washington insists the shipping lanes have been cleared

On Saturday, November 14, the Iranian navy and the Revolutionary Guards claimed that three tankers had hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, in areas banned by Tehran. The US military says it has cleared the main shipping lanes of mines. None of these claims could be independently verified [1][2][3].

According to the Iranian military, fires broke out overnight on three tankers that had entered “unauthorized” areas of the strait; a separate statement from the Revolutionary Guards mentions two ships hit by explosions [1][2].
Another account, reported by Investing.com, mentions at least four ships, including a supertanker. Neither their names nor the extent of the damage have been confirmed [3].

The Iranian navy warns that any “offending” tanker entering the banned area east of the strait “will be set on fire” by naval mines. Since the start of the war in February, Tehran has demanded that ships ask its permission to pass [2].

On the US side, the military says it has cleared the main shipping corridors, and Central Command (Centcom) rejects Iran's version: it says it intercepted two Iranian drones, with no casualties or damage [1][3].
Traffic through the strait remains about 65% below its pre-war level, according to the UK maritime agency UKMTO. The UN counts 134 confirmed maritime incidents in the region since February [3].
At least 25 seafarers have died around Hormuz since February 28, including at least 16 Indians, according to the International Maritime Organization [4].
Oil has not reacted yet: markets were closed. On Friday, Brent ended at $95.84 a barrel, up 2 cents, but down about 2.5% over the week, its second weekly decline in a row [5][6].

Key takeaway: Iran wants to show it is still in control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a large share of the world's oil passes, while the United States claims to have secured it. As long as the two versions clash, shipowners hesitate and traffic stays far below normal [1][3].

Diplomacy is at a standstill. Donald Trump keeps saying the United States does “not need” a deal with Iran [7]. Tehran first demands an end to the US naval blockade of its ports, the lifting of sanctions, the unfreezing of its assets and reparations for war damage [8].
Israel is also hardening its tone: on Saturday, Benjamin Netanyahu said the threat of an Iranian nuclear weapon had to be removed “once and for all” [1].

The paradox: despite these attacks, oil fell this week. Markets are betting on an oversupply, rising OPEC+ output and US inventories, and some are betting that the Democrats' midterm victory will push Washington to end the war [5][6].

Brent remains around $96, far more expensive than before the war: that is what keeps your gasoline and diesel fill-ups at a high level. If markets take the Iranian mines seriously when they reopen on Monday, pump prices could start rising again in the following weeks.

Airbus: Germany wants 16 more A400M military aircraft, a lifeline for a Toulouse program that was short of orders

On Friday, November 13, the German Defense Ministry announced its intention to order 16 additional A400M military transport aircraft from Airbus. This order, made possible by a record defense budget of €139bn for 2027, represents about two years of production for a program whose order book was running dry [1][2][3].
The Federal Defense Ministry announced the planned order of 16 A400Ms on Friday. It explains that the changes voted in the 2027 budget make this purchase possible, without giving the amount [2].
German lawmakers approved a record defense budget of €139bn for 2027, which paves the way for this order, according to Aviation Week [2].

Airbus had just delivered the 53rd and final A400M of Germany's initial order. Sixteen more aircraft represent about two years of production at the current rate, giving Airbus time to find export customers [2][4].
The new aircraft will be tactical versions. They will replace older logistics A400Ms, which Berlin will offer for sale to partner countries [4][5].
France 3 Occitanie speaks of “a second wind for Airbus, which is struggling to maintain the production rate of this model” [1].
The plan had been circulating since late September: the trade press reported at the time that Germany wanted 16 more A400Ms to replace its oldest aircraft [5][6].

This announcement comes the same week as another Airbus project in France: a new 48-hectare plant between Cornebarrieu and Colomiers, northwest of Toulouse, which will employ 3,500 people, including 700 jobs created by 2031 [7].

Key takeaway: the A400M, a European military aircraft that struggled for a long time, is buying time. Its order book was shrinking and Airbus was struggling to keep up the production rate; 16 German aircraft secure about two years of work [1][2].
This is a direct effect of German rearmament. With a defense budget of €139bn, Berlin has the means to fill the order books of European industry, not just American industry [2].
There is also an industrial stake for France: the program is run from Toulouse, and the two years gained give Airbus time to look for export customers to avoid a production gap [1][4].
One step remains: until the contract is signed, the purchase remains a political intention, according to several trade media outlets [2][4].

If you live in Occitanie or work in aerospace, this is good news for jobs: with the future plant near Toulouse, Airbus is confirming its plans in France. More broadly, every European order placed with Airbus rather than with an American competitor keeps defense jobs and skills in Europe.

ASEAN: as the Manila summit opens, Marcos puts energy first, and the South China Sea code of conduct will not be signed

The 49th ASEAN summit opened on Sunday, November 15, in Manila and runs until the 17th. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. put the energy crisis linked to the war in Iran at the top of the priorities. The code of conduct in the South China Sea, “80%” negotiated, will not be signed [1][2][3].

Opening the summit, Ferdinand Marcos Jr. recalled that the crisis had disrupted transport, energy and food, to the point that leaders had considered postponing the previous summit, in Cebu [2]. “We must guarantee the region's energy security,” he declared [2].
“No country can face alone” geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty and the climate, he insisted [4].

The Philippines is urging member countries to ratify an emergency oil-sharing agreement faster; four or five countries have done so, according to Philippine diplomats [5]. The plan for a joint stockpile is still under study, which shows the limits of energy solidarity [6].
In the meantime, the Philippine state-owned company PNOC planned to sign a letter of intent on Saturday with Thai and Indonesian depot operators to build emergency fuel reserves [5][7].

On the South China Sea, Marcos is calling for an “effective and substantive” code of conduct, in line with the 1982 law of the sea [2]. A Philippine official says negotiations are “80%” complete, but a diplomat expects no signing in Manila [1][3].
Nearly 20,000 police officers are deployed around Manila. Donald Trump will only arrive at the end of the summit, and thousands of protesters are expected against him on Tuesday [1].
Key takeaway: Southeast Asia is hit by fuel shortages linked to the war with Iran. The Manila summit is first seeking a joint response to this crisis, ahead of the usual issues [1][6].

The South China Sea code of conduct has been under negotiation for more than twenty years. China and ASEAN have provisionally agreed on about 80% of the text, but remain divided on the area covered and on whether it is binding. The 2026 deadline will be missed [3].
Myanmar remains the other test: leaders are to review the “five-point consensus” adopted after the 2021 coup. Decisions will appear in a negotiated final declaration [6].

When Asia competes for the same oil and gas as Europe, prices rise for everyone, including at the pump in France. The South China Sea is also a major route for container ships delivering electronics and clothing sold in Europe: the slightest crisis there makes shipping more expensive.

Israel: defeated at the polls, Netanyahu calls for a unity government in the name of the Iranian threat, Eisenkot denounces a “PR stunt”

On Saturday, November 14, in a video, outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming Israel's next government, to negotiate a unity government against Iran “without preconditions”. The leader of the Yashar party rejected the offer as “another PR stunt” [1][2][3].
“Let's sit down together without preconditions, set aside our differences and all boycotts, and reach agreements for the security and future of Israel,” Benjamin Netanyahu said [2].

In his view, a narrow government, or one that depended on Arab parties, would be unable to face the Iranian threat. He believes the threat of an Iranian bomb must be removed “once and for all” [1][4].
Gadi Eisenkot replied on X that the negotiating teams had already planned to meet the next day, and that Netanyahu “knows he lost the election” [2][3].

The former chief of staff says he is open to working with Likud and the Religious Zionism party if their commitment to unity is “sincere”, but demands a break with the “extremists”, notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir [5].
Outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich backed Netanyahu's call and urged Eisenkot to accept it [5].
In the October legislative elections, Likud won 27 seats and Yashar 21. Netanyahu's bloc totals 53 seats, Eisenkot's 48 and the Arab parties 19, far from the majority of 61 out of 120 [6].

Key takeaway: it is not Benjamin Netanyahu who holds the mandate to form the government. By brandishing the Iranian threat, he is trying to stay in power in a unity coalition rather than move into opposition [1][2][6].
President Isaac Herzog gave the task to Gadi Eisenkot, recommended by 67 lawmakers, including those of the Arab parties. He has 28 days, extendable by 14, to find a majority [6].

The math remains difficult: the seven seats of the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party are not attached to either camp, and the Arab party Ra'am supports Eisenkot without committing to join his coalition [6]. If both camps fail, Israel would return to the polls in early 2027 [6].
The stakes go beyond Israel: Netanyahu is making Iran the central argument of his offer, a sign that the next government will weigh on the course of the war against the Islamic Republic [1][4].

The makeup of the future Israeli government will weigh on the war with Iran, and therefore on the price of oil and your fuel. A more centrist Eisenkot government could also change the tone of relations with France and Europe, provided it finds a majority by early December.

Ethiopia: the army accuses Eritrea of leading a new offensive by Tigray rebels, with weapons supplied by Egypt

Ethiopian army chief Field Marshal Birhanu Jula says the Tigrayan rebels of the TPLF launched a “fourth wave” of attacks in the Amhara and Afar regions, which he says was repelled. He accuses Eritrea of leading it and Egypt of arming it. Asmara and Cairo have already rejected such accusations [1][2][3].

At a press conference reported on November 14, Birhanu Jula said the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) had targeted military positions in the Amhara and Afar regions, and that the federal army had repelled the attack [1][2].
“The offensive was led by Eritrea, with logistical support and military equipment supplied by Egypt,” he said, without presenting public evidence [1][3].

According to him, the rebel commanders have taken refuge in Eritrea, in Adi Keyh, Mendefera and the capital Asmara. He denounces a coalition bringing together the TPLF, the Amhara Fano militia, the Oromo Liberation Army, Sudan and Egypt, which he says wants to overthrow the government [1].

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty had called the Ethiopian accusations “false” in October [1]. Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel, for his part, accuses Addis Ababa of wanting to seize the Eritrean port of Assab [5].

In late September, Ethiopia had already closed its embassy in Asmara and given 10 Eritrean diplomats 48 hours to leave; Eritrea broke off diplomatic relations, and Egypt and Ethiopia each expelled one of the other's diplomats [4].
On November 13, the US embassy said fighting was continuing in Tigray in remote areas near the Eritrean border, and advised against all travel to Amhara, Tigray and Afar [6].

Key takeaway: nearly four years after the Pretoria peace agreement of November 2022, northern Ethiopia has been at war again since late September, and the conflict is taking on a regional dimension, with Eritrea and Egypt named as enemies by Addis Ababa [1][7].

The conflict has two underlying causes. Ethiopia, landlocked since Eritrea's independence in 1993, wants access to the Red Sea, which Asmara sees as a threat to its sovereignty. And Egypt has opposed Ethiopia's great dam on the Nile for years, while moving closer to Eritrea [1][4].

The human cost is mounting. By late September, at least 150,000 people had fled the fighting in Afar, according to a humanitarian source quoted by AFP [8]. In early November, the UN reported that families who had returned to the Tahtay Adiyabo district, in northwestern Tigray, had to flee again, and that thousands of displaced people were in Debre Birhan (Amhara) and Shire (Tigray) [9].
In Abi Adi, displaced families are still living in classrooms and no longer believe they will return home [7]. No independent verification of Addis Ababa's military claims has been published [1].

The conflict is playing out on the edge of the Red Sea, the route ships take between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal in Egypt. A regional war involving Eritrea and Egypt would further weaken a route already disrupted by the conflict with Iran. For you, this can mean longer delays and higher shipping costs on products imported from Asia.

Indonesia: after Gibran's resignation, Prabowo will choose his new vice president only after the ASEAN and APEC summits

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto announced, on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Manila on November 14 and 15, that he would propose successors to Vice President Gibran, who has resigned, only after the ASEAN and APEC summits. He says he is waiting for “a whisper from God Almighty” to decide [1][2].
Vice President Gibran has resigned; Prabowo Subianto says he will decide on his replacement only once the ASEAN summit in Manila and the APEC summit in Shenzhen are over [1][2].
The president gave no names or criteria. He only said he needed “a whisper from God Almighty” to choose [2].
Under the Constitution, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) must meet within 60 days to elect the new vice president from two candidates proposed by the president [2].
The candidates must come from the parties or coalition that backed the winning presidential ticket in the 2024 election [2].
In the meantime, Prabowo arrived in the Philippines on Saturday, November 14, for the summit, where Indonesia is expected to address the smoke from its forest fires, which pollutes its neighbors [3].
He attended the opening ceremony on Sunday, personally welcomed by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. [4][1].

Key takeaway: Indonesia, Southeast Asia's largest country by population and economy, finds itself without a vice president. Prabowo is taking his time and keeping control: he alone will propose the two names submitted to Parliament [1][2].

The mechanism limits the choice to the parties of the coalition that got Prabowo elected in 2024. The post is therefore becoming a bargaining chip between these parties, each hoping to place one of its own one step away from the presidency [2].

By postponing his decision until after the summits, Prabowo is also sending a message abroad: diplomacy comes first, and the domestic political crisis must not disrupt his presence in Manila and then Shenzhen [1][3].

Indonesia is a major supplier of nickel for electric car batteries and of palm oil. A lasting political crisis could weigh on the rupiah and on these commodities. For now, the transition is taking place within the framework set by the Constitution.

Bitcoin falls 14% in a week and hits $65,000, its lowest since August: fear of a rate hike drives investors away

On Saturday, November 14, bitcoin fell to around $65,000, down about 14% in a week. On Friday, it had already dropped below $70,000, its lowest since August. More than $1bn in leveraged bets were liquidated, and US index funds are losing clients [1][2][4].
Bitcoin was still worth about $74,260 on November 10, according to Fortune [6].
On Friday, November 13, it dropped below $70,000, its lowest level since August, Forbes reports [2].
On Saturday morning, it was hovering around $65,200 after touching about $65,000: the weekend sell-off broke through Friday's low [1].
On Friday, more than $1.3bn in leveraged positions were forcibly liquidated on crypto platforms [4].
US index funds invested in bitcoin recorded net outflows in every session from November 5 to 13 [1].
The decline accelerated after the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday, which sent AI stocks tumbling [1][3].
The next threshold being watched is the August low, at $64,112 [5].
Key takeaway: bitcoin behaves like a very risky tech stock, not like a safe haven. When US rates rise and AI giants fall, it falls even harder. In one week, it lost about 14% [1][3].

The main driver is interest rates. Higher-than-expected US inflation has revived the idea that the Federal Reserve (Fed) could raise its rates. And a risk-free investment that pays more makes an asset with no income, like bitcoin, less attractive [3][4].

The fall feeds on itself. Many buyers borrow to bet on a rise. When the price drops, platforms automatically sell their positions, which pushes the price down further: more than $1.3bn was liquidated this way on Friday [4].
Big investors are pulling back too. Listed funds that hold bitcoin on behalf of savers have seen money flow out day after day since November 5, which removes a major buyer from the market [1][5].

If you hold crypto, be aware that it can lose 14% in a week without any bitcoin-specific news. Leveraged products (where you borrow to bet more) can be liquidated all at once. And for your tax return, a sale at a loss can offset capital gains made on crypto in the same year.

How it works: a crypto “liquidation”

On crypto platforms, you can bet on a rise with borrowed money: this is leverage. With 10x leverage, a 5% rise earns you 50%, but a 10% drop wipes out your entire stake. To avoid losing the money it lent, the platform then automatically sells your position: this is liquidation. The problem is the domino effect. Each forced sale pushes the price down, which triggers other liquidations, and so on. On Friday, more than $1.3bn in positions were liquidated this way [4]. That is why bitcoin can lose several thousand dollars in a few hours, especially on weekends, when few buyers are around [1].

The haul includes 5.07 billion forints ($15.33 million), €2.66 million and $1.26 million [1].

These spectacular seizures help him show that his campaign promises are turning into action, facing a Fidesz that disputes any link with the former minister [1][3].
